e.etymology: From the golden-orange flower, whose name means 'Mary's gold' in honor of the Virgin Mary. It joined the flower names of the late 19th century and is rising again.

assoc.t: marigold, garden flower and Day of the Dead bloom

e.etymology: A modern name used mainly in Mexican and Mexican American families. Its origin is not documented; it is often grouped with Arely and Yaretzi.
Several names share this spelling: a Bulgarian pet form of Slavic names in rad-, 'happy'; the Yiddish Reyna, 'pure'; and a respelling of Reina, Spanish for 'queen'.
A modern American coinage that puts the popular Ja- opening in front of Kai, alongside names like Jakari and Makai. It has no meaning of its own.
The Hawaiian form of Diana, the Roman moon goddess, whose name means 'divine'. On the mainland it also grew out of Qiana, a 1970s fabric name, and is used as a feminine of Kian.
From an Irish surname of Norman origin, traced to a knight called de Leon from Brittany. It is unrelated to the Welsh Dylan, though the two sound alike and are often treated as one name.

assoc.t: Dillon, Texas, fictional town of Friday Night Lights
Marshal Matt Dillon of the TV western Gunsmoke

e.etymology: A spelling of Kylie, a name that arose in Australia, possibly from the Noongar word kylie, 'boomerang'. It is also taken as a feminine form of Kyle.
The masculine of Carmela, from Mount Carmel in Israel, Hebrew karmel, 'garden, orchard'. The name honors Our Lady of Mount Carmel and is traditional in Sicily and Spain.

assoc.t: Carmelo Anthony, NBA star known as Melo

e.etymology: From the surname for someone who lived or worked in a royal forest, Old French forest. Forrest is the more common spelling of the name; this one matches the everyday word.

assoc.t: forest, the everyday word for woodland
Forrest Gump, title character of the 1994 film

e.note: Expect 'Run, Forrest, run!' jokes from the 1994 film Forrest Gump.

e.etymology: From the English word treasure, which comes through Old French tresor from Greek thesauros, 'storehouse'. It is used as a term of endearment and, since the late 20th century, as a given name.
A 20th-century American spelling of Cory, an English and Irish surname of uncertain origin. This spelling is now given mostly to girls.
From Hebrew Eli'el, 'my God is God', built from two words for God. Several minor figures in the Books of Chronicles bear it. In the US it is used mostly in Hispanic families.
From a Scottish place name and clan surname, probably from a Brittonic word for 'wood'. It became a first name in the 19th century and peaked in the US in the 1960s.
A Czech, Slovak and Belarusian form of Helena, also a short form of Magdalena. Helen is a Greek name of uncertain meaning, often linked to words for 'torch' or 'light'.
From the affectionate word for a little bird, also an old pet form of Bertha and Elizabeth. It was a top-1000 US girls' name from 1880 to about 1940 and has returned in the 2020s.

assoc.t: birdie, golf score of one under par

e.etymology: From Tagalog malaya, 'free, independent'. Malaya is also the historical name of the Malay Peninsula, and in the US the name sits beside Malia and Malaysia.

assoc.t: Malaya, former name of peninsular Malaysia

e.meaning: he who holds firm the good
e.etymology: From the Latin and Greek forms of Old Persian Darayavaush, 'he who holds firm the good'. Three Persian kings bore it, including Darius the Great, who appears in the Bible.
namesakes: Darius Rucker (Hootie & the Blowfish singer and country star)
Darius the Great (king of ancient Persia)

e.etymology: A pet form of Charlotte, the French feminine of Charles, from a Germanic word for a free man. Common around 1900, it is back in fashion in Britain and rising in the US.
A late 20th-century American coinage, a variant of Jaylene, joining Jay to the -leen ending of names like Kathleen and Eileen.

An English name on record since the 1500s, also spelled Amyas. Its source is uncertain: it may come from the medieval name Amis, from Latin amicus, 'friend', or from a surname for someone from Amiens in France.
From Hebrew Netan'el, 'God has given', through the Greek of the New Testament, where Nathanael is a disciple of Jesus in John's Gospel. Nathaniel is the more common English spelling.
The Italian form of Vincent, from Latin Vincentius, from vincere, 'to conquer'.
From Old French, the name of a 3rd-century martyr, Latin Quintinus, a derivative of Quintus, 'fifth', once given to a fifth child. The Normans brought it to England.
A respelling of Rowan, the English form of Irish Ruadhan, 'little red-haired one', and also the name of the rowan tree with its red berries.
From Arabic zayd, from the root z-y-d, 'to increase'. Zayd ibn Harithah, the adopted son of the Prophet Muhammad, is the only companion named in the Quran.
From the Irish surname O Floinn, 'descendant of Flann', a byname meaning 'red' or 'ruddy'.

assoc.t: Flynn Rider, hero of Disney's Tangled
Errol Flynn, swashbuckling film star (in like Flynn)

e.etymology: A Dutch short form of Koenraad (Conrad), 'bold counsel'; koen is also the Dutch word for 'brave'. Many American parents use it as a spelling of Cohen.
e.note: In the US usually said KOH-en, like Cohen, a Jewish priestly surname that some find inappropriate as a first name.

e.etymology: From the Cheyenne people of the Great Plains. Their English name came through French from Dakota Sioux shahiyena, a term for people whose speech the Dakota could not understand.

assoc.t: the Cheyenne, Native American nation of the Plains

e.note: Also the name of a living Native American nation; some people object to its use as a baby name.

e.etymology: From Hebrew Elisha, 'my God is salvation'. In the Books of Kings he is the prophet who succeeds Elijah. Girls given the name usually say it like Alicia.
namesakes: Elisha Cuthbert (actress, 24 and The Girl Next Door)

e.etymology: A short form of Tracy, a Norman surname from a place in France named for a Gallo-Roman called Thracius. It also matches the everyday word trace.
A respelling of Wilder, an English surname from Old English wilde, 'wild, untamed', for someone who lived on uncultivated land or had a wild streak.
A shortened form of Leonora, itself from Eleonora, the Italian form of Eleanor. Eleanor goes back to the Provencal name Alienor, borne by Eleanor of Aquitaine; its meaning is uncertain.
